data.analysis: Keep N=3 and preserve all roles: the source supports three useful but distinct hypotheses—axis-state reuse, scalar hot-path restructuring, and vectorization across pixels. The critique found no basis for assuming any one dominates: only end-to-end baseline measurements are available, not a cost breakdown. T1’s scratch-memory traffic could erase savings; T2 and T3 both touch the Noise/Grad path; and vector gathers may not outperform scalar table lookup. Revise objectives to call for controlled variants against the same baseline, separate measurement of major sub-approaches, and explicit treatment of hybrid experiments as hypotheses rather than prohibited work. The GCC 14.2 manual documents loop-vectorization behavior, but the frozen build flags are unknown: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc-14.2.0/gcc/Optimize-Options.html.

revisions.objective: Test whether per-axis, per-octave state reuse reduces total runtime enough to justify its scratch traffic. Compare the scalar baseline with staged variants—for example, storing only lattice/fraction state, then additionally storing smooth weights and shared z state. Preserve the original coordinate-expression order and octave progression. Include allocation and state access in timing; validate n=768 and smaller/shifted bounds at the fixed tolerance. Keep hybrid variants separately identified and measured, and record unsuccessful layouts or attempts.
revisions.subject: Per-axis, per-octave coordinate-state reuse

revisions.objective: Test scalar-only restructuring of the per-pixel Noise/Grad path. Measure hash-addressing/gradient-selection changes separately from interpolation-polynomial and octave-control-flow changes, so the source of any gain or regression is visible. Use the original scalar implementation as the controlled comparison; correctness-preserving combinations remain possible but should be measured separately. Validate all specified checks and the fixed tolerance, and record failed approaches. Do not assume arithmetic rewrites or table changes will be faster.
revisions.subject: Scalar Perlin hash, gradient, and interpolation kernel

revisions.objective: Test whether mapping adjacent output pixels to SIMD lanes improves end-to-end time on the frozen build and target. Compare explicit SIMD—including the cost of dependent permutation-table gathers—with a simpler compiler-vectorizable formulation where feasible; first preserve the scalar per-lane math to isolate vectorization, then label any further kernel rewrites as separate variants. Do not assume the manual’s vectorization defaults match the actual build flags or that a wider vector is faster. Include tails and full-call costs, validate all specified bounds and sizes at the fixed tolerance, and record failed implementations.
revisions.subject: SIMD across independent image pixels

data.shared_assumptions: All three hypotheses infer potential cost from the repeated eight-octave scalar source; the only performance evidence is the valid baseline’s three 768-size timings, not a kernel breakdown. Scratch overhead, dependent permutation lookups, and vectorization effectiveness are unmeasured. T1 and T2 can interact in the scalar loop, and T2 and T3 can alter the same hot path, so isolated measurements do not establish additive gains. Keep the same one-core target, frozen build/protocol, complete-output behavior, fixed tolerance, and valid-input coverage; compare the actual integrated candidate and require independent final confirmation.
